The Female.
That anaconda was a female, and so is every giant anaconda you have ever pictured.
Over seven years in Venezuela, the biologist Jesús Rivas and his team caught and measured seven hundred and eighty wild anacondas.
The heaviest male in the whole study weighed just seventeen.
A grown female averages almost five times the weight of a grown male,
the biggest size gap between the sexes reported in any land animal with a backbone.
Picture a couple where one weighs as much as a grown man and the other weighs about as much as a packed suitcase.
Here's the twist.
In twenty twenty-four, a team led by Rivas compared anaconda genes from nine countries
and argued that the green anaconda is really two species.
In the genes they compared, the northern and southern snakes differ by about five and a half percent,
after splitting roughly ten million years ago.
For now, the main reptile checklist still counts them as one species.
If the split holds, the heaviest snake on Earth was quietly two different snakes,
and scientists are still arguing about her name.

The Nostrils.
A green anaconda's eyes and nostrils sit on top of its head,
so it can breathe and watch while almost all of it stays underwater.
At first glance, the pool is empty, which is exactly the plan.
The anaconda is an ambush hunter, and it lies in the shallows with only its snout above the surface,
waiting for something to come down to drink.
A thin, clear scale covers each eye,
which helps it see underwater and keeps the eye safe from the brush on land.
When it does go fully under, it can stay submerged for about ten minutes before it needs those nostrils again.
From the bank, all you see is two bumps the size of olives on a log that isn't a log.
In the dry season on the Venezuelan plains, the water shrinks,
and the anacondas gather in whatever pools are left.
The unsettling part is the menu.
Rivas described them as opportunists that will take any prey they can kill and swallow.
The snake does not care what comes to the water, as long as something does.

The Breeding Ball.
The same dry season that crowds anacondas into the last pools is also when they breed,
and it does not look romantic.
One female ends up wrapped in a slow, writhing ball of males.
Rivas found balls with anywhere from one to thirteen males, and three was typical.
The balls he timed lasted eighteen days on average, and the longest went on for forty-six.
Individual males hung on for about two weeks, and some stayed for more than a month.
Imagine a knot of garden hoses the size of a bathtub, and every single hose is trying to be first.
Size is the prize here, because larger females are courted by more males,
and they give birth to more babies, and bigger ones.
The darkest part is what happens afterwards.
A pregnant female does not eat for about seven months.
Females have also been found eating males around the breeding balls,
and Rivas suggested that some may eat a partner to help get through that long fast.
Doug wades in with a whistle to break it up, but every snake is busy.

The Teeth.
The anaconda has no venom.
What it has instead is six rows of sharp teeth, four along the top of the mouth and two along the bottom,
and every one of them points backwards.
It strikes from the water, seizes the prey with those teeth, and drags it under.
The teeth are fixed in place, with no folding fangs and no poison doing the work, so they simply hold on.
The teeth work like a fish hook, where going in is easy and backing out is not.
But that's not what the bite is for.
The bite is not meant to kill anything.
It's there so the prey can't leave while the rest of the snake arrives,
and it matters, because some of this prey bites back.
Capybaras have razor-sharp front teeth, and Rivas found female anacondas carrying scars that matched capybara bites.
He once found a female constricting a young capybara in the bushes while an adult capybara stood nearby, staring at the spot.
The anaconda's answer is to bite first and never let go.

The Coils.
For a long time, people said constrictors kill by suffocation,
and in a close relative, the boa constrictor, that turned out to be wrong.
In a twenty fifteen study, researchers measured what happens inside an anesthetized lab rat while a boa squeezes it.
Within six seconds, the blood pressure in an artery in its leg had fallen by half,
while the pressure in the big veins near its heart went up sixfold.
Within a minute its heart rate had nearly halved.
By the end of the squeeze, the heart was beating almost four times slower, because it was pushing against a pressure it could not beat.
Here's the problem.
The prey does not die from running out of air, because its blood stops moving first.
An animal can last a while without a breath, but not without a pulse, which is exactly why this is so much faster.
The study used boas, but its authors argued that killing this way gave all constrictors, anacondas included, an edge.
Being constricted is like a blood pressure cuff that keeps on inflating long after it beeps.

The Heartbeat.
A constrictor can feel its prey's heartbeat, and it decides when to stop by paying attention to it.
In a twenty twelve study, boas squeezed dead rats that had been fitted with an artificial heart.
While the heart was beating, the snakes squeezed longer and harder than they did when there was no heartbeat at all.
When the researchers stopped the heart halfway through, the snakes let go soon after.
Even snakes that had never caught live prey did it, so it seems to be at least partly built in.
The snake is a smartwatch that only switches off when your pulse does.
The worst part is that the squeeze barely gets in the way of the snake's own breathing.
You would expect a squeeze like that to make breathing hard for the snake, too.
But in a twenty twenty-two study, researchers wrapped a blood pressure cuff around part of a boa,
and it simply switched to breathing with ribs further along its body.
It can squeeze with one part of itself and breathe with another.

The Jaws.
People say a snake dislocates its jaw to swallow big prey, but it really doesn't.
The two halves of an anaconda's lower jaw are not fused at the chin.
They're joined by elastic ligaments that stretch,
and the jaw bones hinge loosely on the skull, so the mouth opens far wider than the head looks.
Then it walks its jaws forward over the meal, one side at a time, while the teeth on the other side hold on.
A big swallow can take a long time, so the snake can push the end of its windpipe forward and to the side,
and keep breathing around a full mouth.
Rivas recorded anacondas eating capybaras and deer,
and he wrote that they can take prey as big as a grown capybara, a grown deer, or a full-grown caiman, up to around seventy kilos.
Swallowing a capybara is like a garden hose swallowing a beach ball, slowly, without a straw.

The Caiman.
Anacondas eat spectacled caimans, small crocodilian relatives of alligators that share their pools.
In nineteen ninety-nine, a snake about four and a half meters long was seen constricting a spectacled caiman nearly two meters long,
and Rivas wrote that anacondas catch caimans often on the Venezuelan plains.
An anaconda swallowing a caiman is like a sleeping bag swallowing a suitcase full of knives.
But here's the catch.
It goes both ways, and over seven years, Rivas's team found twelve dead anacondas,
and the bite marks showed that caimans had killed at least eight of them, including every male.
